title: Reseña de Políticas de Educación Superior en América Latina: Expansión, Diversificación y Equidad, por André Vieira, Andrés Santos Sharpe, Carolina Zuccarelli and María Lígia Barbosa (Comps.)
text_snippet: Reseña de Políticas de Educación Superior en América Latina: Expansión, Diversificación y Equidad, por André Vieira, Andrés Santos Sharpe, Carolina Zuccarelli and María Lígia Barbosa (Comps.) Esta obra ofrece un análisis multidimensional sobre el proceso de masificación de la matrícula del nivel superior en América Latina, abordando tanto las tendencias regionales comunes como las particularidades históricas e institucionales de Brasil, Uruguay, Perú, Argentina y Chile. A través de ocho capítulos organizados en tres ejes temáticos (Fundamentación y contexto, Estructura institucional y Funcionamiento), el libro reúne investigaciones que utilizan principalmente el análisis comparado y estudios empíricos para desentrañar las dinámicas de expansión educativa. Los trabajos aquí reunidos constituyen un aporte importante sobre las tendencias pasadas y presentes de la educación superior en la región, permitiendo una comprensión precisa de cómo operan los mecanismos de estratificación social en el ámbito universitario latinoamericano.

title: Review of Dialogic Feedback in the Age of Algorithmic Governance: Key to PCP-Coaching and Assessment-as-Learning, by Filip Dochy et al.
text_snippet: Review of Dialogic Feedback in the Age of Algorithmic Governance: Key to PCP-Coaching and Assessment-as-Learning, by Filip Dochy et al. Dialogic Feedback for High Impact Learning reframes feedback as a relational and dialogic process grounded in Assessment-as-Learning, offering a persuasive challenge to compliance-driven, transmission-based models of evaluation. This review examines the book's central contributions—dialogic feedback as relational practice, feedback literacy, and learner agency—alongside its limitations, including an underspecified audience and limited engagement with the sociotechnical conditions reshaping contemporary feedback systems. The review extends the dialogic framework into the domain of algorithmic governance, arguing that the three conditions Dochy and colleagues identify as essential to meaningful feedback—interpretive openness, relational accountability, and shared authority—are precisely those that AI-mediated evaluation systems tend to suppress. The book's most consequential contribution may be one it does not develop directly: it supplies the normative vocabulary needed to evaluate and challenge automated feedback infrastructures. Whether dialogic feedback can survive the turn toward automation is ultimately a question about power.

title: Review Of Effective Multimodal Interaction for Online and Hybrid Teaching: Data Driven Insights, by Antonella Giacosa
text_snippet: Review Of Effective Multimodal Interaction for Online and Hybrid Teaching: Data Driven Insights, by Antonella Giacosa This book explores how global education systems adapted to online and hybrid learning in response to the COVID-19 pandemic. The author discusses the concepts of Emergency Remote Teaching (ERT) and electronic Classroom Interactional Competence (e-CIC) as well as the dynamics of multimodal interaction in digital learning environments encompassing text, voice, visuals, emojis, and other communication channels. Through a mixed-methods approach combining ethnography, conversation analysis, and multimodality, the author examines three primary learning modes asynchronous, synchronous, and hybrid along with their respective pedagogical opportunities and challenges. Key findings indicate that the success of online learning is not determined solely by the technological platform, but rather by the quality of pedagogical design, teachers' digital competence, and the ability to construct social presence in virtual spaces. The findings also emphasize institutional readiness gaps and teachers' unpreparedness in facing the sudden digitalization of education. title: Review of Innovations in International Student Enrollment: Global Strategies, Digital Transformation, and Emerging Perspectives, by Clay Harmon and Krishna Bista (Eds.)
text_snippet: Review of Innovations in International Student Enrollment: Global Strategies, Digital Transformation, and Emerging Perspectives, by Clay Harmon and Krishna Bista (Eds.) This edited volume examines the evolving landscape of international student enrollment in higher education, foregrounding the interplay between digital transformation, policy shifts, and student experiences. Drawing on global case studies from the United States, Asia, Africa, and Latin America, the book explores how institutions respond to geopolitical uncertainty, demographic changes, and technological advancements. The contributors highlight the importance of inclusive practices, strategic enrollment management, and culturally responsive support systems in fostering student success. Through interdisciplinary perspectives, the volume emphasizes that international enrollment is not merely a recruitment exercise but a complex ecosystem shaped by socio-political, economic, and institutional forces. It offers practical insights for policymakers, educators, and administrators seeking to balance innovation with equity, demonstrating that sustainable internationalization depends on aligning technological progress with human-centered approaches to student engagement and belonging.

title: Review of The Highest Exam: How the Gaokao Shapes China, by Ruixue Jia & Hongbin Li, with Claire Cousineau
text_snippet: Review of The Highest Exam: How the Gaokao Shapes China, by Ruixue Jia & Hongbin Li, with Claire Cousineau This volume is the first book-length, data-driven account for a general audience of China’s national college entrance examination - the gaokao, popularly understood to be the last remaining channel for social advancement.

title: Review of Crafting Ethical Scholarship: A Practical Guide to Academic Integrity and the Mission of Higher Education, by K. E. Kessler et al.
text_snippet: Review of Crafting Ethical Scholarship: A Practical Guide to Academic Integrity and the Mission of Higher Education, by K. E. Kessler et al. In Crafting Ethical Scholarship: A Practical Guide to Academic Integrity and the Mission of Higher Education, authors Kessler, Michiels, and Rogers challenge compliance-based approaches to academic integrity and instead present scholarship as a developmental, communal, and ethical practice. Drawing on research into expert writing, disciplinary enculturation, and scholarly identity formation, the book argues that academic integrity is best understood as a process of becoming rather than merely a set of rules governing misconduct. The review evaluates the book's contributions to higher education, faculty development, writing instruction, and student success initiatives, while considering its relevance in an era increasingly shaped by generative artificial intelligence.

title: Review of Invent Ed: How an American Tradition of Innovation Can Transform College Today, by Caroline F. Levander
text_snippet: Review of Invent Ed: How an American Tradition of Innovation Can Transform College Today, by Caroline F. Levander Invent Ed offers a provocative look at the role of the arts and humanities in innovative thinking, and their place within the structure of higher education today. In her work, Levander utilizes a historical perspective to make the claim that the integration of multiple disciplines is necessary, and yet lacking, within our modern educational system. Her argument is compelling, given the history she presents, current public consternation about the value proposition of higher education, and the recent impact of AI in industry and education.

title: Review of Segregation and School Funding: How States Reinforce Inequality and What to Do About It, by M. Di Carlo & B. D. Baker
text_snippet: Review of Segregation and School Funding: How States Reinforce Inequality and What to Do About It, by M. Di Carlo & B. D. Baker In this book, Matthew DiCarlo and Bruce Baker examine how racial and economic segregation in U.S. public schools is tied directly to the way schools are funded. The authors intersperse discussion of historical milestones toward equity and their marginal effectiveness with illustrative case studies of school districts in seven metropolitan areas. They also discuss some little-known history that underpins the persistent problem of inequitable education in the United States metropolitan areas. This well-reasoned and well-documented book is an important contribution to the larger, longstanding, and continuously evolving conversation about civil rights, educational equity, housing segregation, tax policy and public-school reform.

title: Review of Critical Thinking for Medical and Graduate Students, by Jonathan M. Berman, Troy Camarata, and Tony A. Slieman
text_snippet: Review of Critical Thinking for Medical and Graduate Students, by Jonathan M. Berman, Troy Camarata, and Tony A. Slieman This book addresses the gap between memorizing facts and using them in high-stakes clinical moments. The authors use dual-process theory to define critical thinking as "System 2" reasoning. This deliberate reflection is treated as a core professional skill rather than an optional add-on. Focusing on metacognition and cognitive biases, the authors explain how mental shortcuts like availability and confirmation bias lead to systematic diagnostic errors. A key strengthof the book is its practical strategies, such as information triage, which help students organize data into mental models called "schemata". This review explores the relationship between general thinking skills and domain-specific expertise. While the book provides an excellent foundation, it raises questions about how much context matters in clinical reasoning. The article emphasizes that teaching critical thinking requires a culture that supports reflection over speed. Ultimately, the text encourages a mindset of scientific skepticism and self-awareness. These traits are essential for navigating the uncertainty of modern medicine.

title: Review of Being in Shadow and Light: Academics in Post/Conflict Higher Education, by Dina Zoe Belluigi (Ed.)
text_snippet: Review of Being in Shadow and Light: Academics in Post/Conflict Higher Education, by Dina Zoe Belluigi (Ed.) In Being in Shadow and Light: Academics in Post/Conflict Higher Education, Editor Dina Zoe Belluigi and contributors shift attention from institutional reconstruction and policy reform toward the lived experiences of academics working in conflict and post-conflict higher education contexts. It explores how academics teach, remember, archive, resist, and produce knowledge under conditions shaped by violence, displacement, censorship, institutional silence, and historical trauma. This review highlights the book’s conceptual contribution through the interpretive framework of shadow and light, its methodological plurality, and its relevance to higher education studies, postcolonial theory, academic freedom, peace and conflict studies, and critical pedagogy. Overall, the book is a significant contribution to understanding academic subjectivity, educational responsibility, and knowledge production in contexts marked by unresolved conflict.

title: Review of Fair Game: Trans Athletes and the Future of Sports, by Ellie Roscher and Anna Baeth
text_snippet: Review of Fair Game: Trans Athletes and the Future of Sports, by Ellie Roscher and Anna Baeth In their book Fair Game, Ellie Roscher and Anna Baeth address and dispel myths about transgender athletes and their inclusion to sports as a whole. The authors’ primary argument is that trans athletes do not pose a significant risk to the world of sports and that they may indeed offer new perspectives on the gendered way we approach sports at the present. This text is a timely response to the increasing attempts across the United States to legislate trans athletes off the field and out of public sports.

title: Review of Slow Violence: Confronting Dark Truths in the American Classroom, by Ranita Ray
text_snippet: Review of Slow Violence: Confronting Dark Truths in the American Classroom, by Ranita Ray The heart of this book is an unwavering showing of “slow violence,” and there is something for scholars across several research domains. As a study of schools, Slow Violence is grounded in the quotidian of student-teacher relations. Professor Ray offers social psychologists a brilliant study of affect, shame as social control, role identities, social exchange, and identity destruction. Slow Violence is also an examination of how institutional pressures and organizational cultures can be harmful. Researchers dedicated to the study and uprooting of racism could read Slow Violence as a race-forward book.

title: Review of Coaching Education Leaders: A Culturally Responsive Approach to Transforming Schools and Systems, by Nancy Gutierrez, Michelle Jarney and Michael Kim
text_snippet: Review of Coaching Education Leaders: A Culturally Responsive Approach to Transforming Schools and Systems, by Nancy Gutierrez, Michelle Jarney and Michael Kim In Coaching Education Leaders: A Culturally Responsive Approach to Transforming Schools and Systems, Gutierrez, Jarney and Kim reconceptualize leadership coaching as an equity-centered and relational process designed to foster systemic transformation rather than isolated professional improvement. This review examines the authors’ facilitative competency-based coaching framework and analyzes its contributions to contemporary conversations surrounding culturally responsive leadership, educator identity development, and organizational change. Particular attention is given to the text’s emphasis on reflective practice, relational trust, equity leadership dispositions, and the interconnected nature of coaching across individuals and institutions. The review also explores the authors’ treatment of feedback, dialogue, and authentic leadership spaces, including the metaphorical concept of “the kitchen” as a site of vulnerability and transformational learning. While the book offers a compelling and practitioner-oriented framework for equity-driven coaching, this review critiques the limited empirical grounding supporting the proposed model and questions the sustainability of such approaches

title: What Is It That I Have Become? Some Fragments [Acquired Wisdom Essay]
text_snippet: What Is It That I Have Become? Some Fragments [Acquired Wisdom Essay] There are many ways to write oneself. Most popular is the story—a life lived, experiences accumulated, lessons learned, wisdom acquired, triumph or tragedy—a coherent and linear self. I do not want to do that. That is a fiction. Rather, I offer some fragments, some discontinuities, and some tensions and paradoxes that make up what might be called my biography. I want to think about “what it is I have become.” And I will do that against the backdrop of the epistemic shift that has framed and forged my intellectual career—the shift from a welfare state to a neoliberal state, from one form of domination to another, an intensification. I will try to make sense of myself as a social subject, as produced contingently and historically across that shift, and allude to some struggles and resistance to not being governed thus—another kind of fiction perhaps. This will encompass both my experience of education, very briefly at school and at university and the evolution and reorientations of my intellectual preoccupations as a researcher and “scholar.” There is a class, social class, sub-text to some of this; but I will not dwell on that. title: Review of We Are Who We’re Waiting For: Transformative Change in Early Childhood Education, by Kisa Marx
text_snippet: Review of We Are Who We’re Waiting For: Transformative Change in Early Childhood Education, by Kisa Marx Kisa Marx's We Are Who We're Waiting For is a revolutionary text that defies easy categorization. Part memoir, part pedagogical manifesto, part unapologetic love letter to Black children, this work weaves together personal narrative, critical theory, and practical wisdom into what can only be described as an instrumental autobiographical text for educators. Marx has created something rare in educational literature: a book that not only espouses transformative practices but models them in its very structure and voice.

title: Review of Undeclared: A Philosophy of Formative Higher Education, by Chris Higgins
text_snippet: Review of Undeclared: A Philosophy of Formative Higher Education, by Chris Higgins This book offers a sustained philosophical critique of contemporary higher education and articulates a compelling alternative grounded in formative learning. Drawing on philosophy of education, moral philosophy, and cultural criticism, Chris Higgins interrogates the corporatization, instrumentalization, and credentialism that dominate modern universities. Structured as three extended essays and reflective interludes, Higgins reconceptualizes higher education as a space for the formation of persons rather than the production of market-ready credentials. He develops the notion of “formative higher education” as an existential and ethical project, emphasizing integrity, aesthetic education, and humane vocation. Combining philosophical argument with literary, historical, and institutional analysis, this book resists technocratic solutions and instead reclaims education as a lived, meaning-making practice. Overall, the work makes a significant contribution to debates on the aims of higher education and the future of liberal learning.

title: Review of The Eclipse of Reason: Reclaiming Western Education for Today, by Wilfred Carr
text_snippet: Review of The Eclipse of Reason: Reclaiming Western Education for Today, by Wilfred Carr In this insightful review, Bob Stake asks readers to consider the following question: "If Education is the question, is Reasoning the answer?"

title: Review of Improving a Country’s Education: PISA 2018 Results in 10 Countries, by Nuno Crato (Ed.)
text_snippet: Review of Improving a Country’s Education: PISA 2018 Results in 10 Countries, by Nuno Crato (Ed.) This edited book analyzes international educational performance using PISA 2018 data, focusing on how different national education systems influence student achievement. Through comparative case studies of several countries that show how improvements in educational outcomes depend not only on financial investment but also on the coherence between curriculum design, assessment systems, and education policy implementation, the book highlights the importance of policy consistency, institutional stability, and system-wide alignment in achieving effective educational reform. It also critically addresses the limitations of PISA data in explaining causality, emphasizing the need to complement international assessments with national-level evidence and contextual analysis.

title: Review of Brothers in Grief: The Hidden Toll of Gun Violence on Black Boys and Their Schools, by Nora Gross
text_snippet: Review of Brothers in Grief: The Hidden Toll of Gun Violence on Black Boys and Their Schools, by Nora Gross Brothers in Grief by Nora Gross is a poignant, deeply moving ethnographic account of the untimely and violent deaths of Black boys that have occured in a short time span at the elite, charter school, Boys' Prep in Philadelphia. Gross's book sheds light on societal violence, especially in Philadelphia, structural barriers to grief in educational institutions, and racialized masculinity leading to stoicism and repression of emotional expression among Black males.

title: Review of Sanctuary School: Innovating to Empower Immigrant Youth, by Chandler Patton Miranda
text_snippet: Review of Sanctuary School: Innovating to Empower Immigrant Youth, by Chandler Patton Miranda This review highlights the book’s significance for contemporary discussions of immigrant justice, school climate, belonging, and equity-centered school design, with particular attention to sanctuary as both a policy orientation and a set of educational practices for immigrant-impacted students. This timely and consequential volume will be of interest to scholars, teacher educators, and school leaders concerned with educational equity and immigrant-origin youth.

title: Review of Teaching from an Ethical Center: Practical Wisdom for Daily Instruction, by Cara Furman
text_snippet: Review of Teaching from an Ethical Center: Practical Wisdom for Daily Instruction, by Cara Furman In this highly readable book about teaching and ethics, Cara Furman weaves philosophical ideas together with examples of teaching practices so that philosophy illuminates the teaching practices, giving them both a new depth. Rather than an abstract treatise about philosophical concepts, Teaching from an Ethical Center is a practical book for teacher educators, teachers, and philosophers of education to explore and articulate their own teaching goals.

title: Review of Epistemological Beliefs and Critical Thinking in Mathematics, by Benjamin Rott
text_snippet: Review of Epistemological Beliefs and Critical Thinking in Mathematics, by Benjamin Rott A major issue in mathematics education is students’ tendency to focus on obtaining correct answers without understanding the reasoning process. Benjamin Rott explores this issue in his book, Epistemological Belief and Critical Thinking in Mathematics. The book emphasizes the importance of deep understanding, reflection, and the use of assessment methods that can effectively capture students’ cognitive processes during mathematics learning. For Rott, the development of critical thinking in mathematics depends more on the quality of argumentation and reasoning processes than on final answers or the beliefs themselves.

title: Review of Reading Assessment Done Right: Tools and Techniques for Data-Driven Instruction, by Stephanie Stollar & Kate Winn
text_snippet: Review of Reading Assessment Done Right: Tools and Techniques for Data-Driven Instruction, by Stephanie Stollar & Kate Winn In Reading Assessment Done Right, Stollar and Winn seek to reposition reading assessment as a tool for instructional decision-making rather than compliance. The authors argue for the use of assessments that generate actionable data and provide a structured framework for interpreting results and adjusting instruction. This review examines the clarity and practicality of that framework, particularly the use of the Collaborative Improvement Cycle and the emphasis on distinguishing between useful and non-useful data. While the book offers strong guidance for interpreting assessment results, this review highlights the challenges of implementing these recommendations within real classroom and district constraints and the gap between well-designed assessment systems and their practical use.

title: Review of Reading and Writing for Pleasure: A Framework for Practice, by Teresa Cremin et al.
text_snippet: Review of Reading and Writing for Pleasure: A Framework for Practice, by Teresa Cremin et al. In this volume, Cremin et al. explore why enjoyment matters in helping students become readers and writers and encourage teachers to move beyond a skills-only focus and create classroom environments where students genuinely want to read and write. Drawing on classroom connections and reflection, they consider how making space for choice, engagement, and meaningful experiences can shape how students see themselves as readers and writers. The emphasis is that pleasure is not an extra, but an important part of supporting lifelong literacy.

title: Review of The New College Classroom, by Cathy N. Davidson & Christina Katopodis
text_snippet: Review of The New College Classroom, by Cathy N. Davidson & Christina Katopodis In The New College Classroom, authors Davidson and Katopodis translate cutting-edge research in learning science and pedagogy into ready-to-use strategies that instructors in any discipline may incorporate into their courses to create an environment that is truly conducive to learning. These empirically driven, classroom-tested techniques of active learning―from the participatory syllabus and ungrading to grab-and-go activities for every day of the term―have achieved impressive results at community colleges and research universities, on campus, online, and in hybrid settings. Davidson and Katopodis explain how and why their approach is more effective than conventional methods of instruction and provide detailed case studies of educators successfully applying active-learning techniques in their courses every day, ensuring that their students are better prepared for the world after college.

title: Review of Undeclared: A Philosophy of Formative Higher Education, by Chris Higgins
text_snippet: Review of Undeclared: A Philosophy of Formative Higher Education, by Chris Higgins Undeclared—a volume consisting of three major essays linked by shorter interludes—addresses a single question: What would it mean for higher education to take human formation seriously?

title: Review of The Safetyfication of Education: Neoliberalism, Psychopolitics and the End of Critical Education, by Marta Estellés
text_snippet: Review of The Safetyfication of Education: Neoliberalism, Psychopolitics and the End of Critical Education, by Marta Estellés English and Spanish versions of Diego Palacios's review of The Safetyfication of Education, an open access book in which author Marta Estellés examines the dominance of safety discourses in education and its connection with neoliberalism.
